Communicability sums the walks of every length k divided by k factorial, 2/2! + 1/3! + 15/4! and so on, giving 2.069 for B and E." width="100%"} Communicability measures the "amount of communication" between pairs of nodes based on all walks between them, with shorter walks weighted more heavily. It uses the matrix exponential of the adjacency matrix: `exp(A)`. For nodes `u` and `v`, the communicability is: `C(u, v) = \\sum_{j=1}^{n} \\phi_j(u) \\phi_j(v) e^{\\lambda_j}` where :math:`\\phi_j` are eigenvectors and :math:`\\lambda_j` are eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict[int, dict[int, float]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Nested dictionary where `result[u][v]` is the communicability between nodes `u` and `v`. Values are positive between nodes in the same connected component and exactly `0` between nodes in different components, which no walk joins. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is directed or has self-loops. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Communicability, introduced by Estrada and Hatano (2008), weights every walk between two nodes by an exponentially decaying factor of its length: $C(u, v) = \sum_{k \ge 0} \dfrac{(A^k)_{uv}}{k!} = (\exp A)_{uv}$. Expanding $\exp A$ in the eigenbasis $A = \sum_j \lambda_j \phi_j \phi_j^\top$ gives the working formula $C(u, v) = \sum_j \phi_j(u)\, \phi_j(v)\, e^{\lambda_j}$, which is what the implementation actually computes through a single dense eigendecomposition. The whole procedure costs $O(n^3)$ time and $O(n^2)$ space, so it comfortably scales to a few thousand nodes. Because $A$ is symmetric for undirected graphs, so is the result: $C(u, v) = C(v, u)$. Self-values $C(u, u)$ are always strictly positive and are known separately as the subgraph centrality. Directed graphs and self-loops are rejected because their matrix exponentials have different structural interpretations. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Adjacent nodes have more walks connecting them than nodes two hops apart, so their communicability score comes out higher: ::: {#2a20840b .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec # Create a path graph: 1 -- 2 -- 3 graph = ec.Graph(directed=False) graph.add_nodes(["1", "2", "3"]) graph.add_edges([("1", "2"), ("2", "3")]) comm = graph.communicability() id1 = graph.get_id_from_label("1") id2 = graph.get_id_from_label("2") id3 = graph.get_id_from_label("3") comm[id1][id2], comm[id1][id3] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (1.3682988720085911, 0.5890917783042856) ``` ::: ::: Summing a node's communicability with every other node gives a sense of how well connected it is overall -- unsurprisingly high for a hub: ::: {#50191fd1 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph(directed=False) graph.add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) graph.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("B", "D")]) comm = graph.communicability() b_id = graph.get_id_from_label("B") sum(comm[b_id].values()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 7.656337130875942 ``` ::: :::
